rubric.why: Identifies chromatin as the uncondensed, thread-like material in the nucleus.
rubric.description: Describes chromatin as a thread-like network of DNA and proteins.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying chromatin as thread-like or network-like material.

rubric.why: Explains that chromatin condenses to form distinct chromosomes during cell division.
rubric.description: Distinguishes chromosomes as condensed, distinct structures formed from chromatin.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing chromosomes as condensed chromatin or noting their formation during cell division.

modelAnswer: Chromatin is a fine, thread-like network of DNA and proteins present in the nucleus, usually when the cell is not dividing.
During cell division, chromatin condenses into distinct, visible chromosomes that carry genes.

items.followUp: State two differences between plant and animal cells.

rubric.why: Protein synthesis is the main function of ribosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying protein synthesis as their function.

rubric.why: Ribosomes translate genetic instructions to assemble amino acids into proteins.
rubric.description: Explains that ribosomes assemble amino acids into proteins according to genetic instructions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing translation or the assembly of amino acids into a protein.

modelAnswer: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis in the cell.
They translate genetic instructions and join amino acids together to form proteins.

items.followUp: Write the scientific names of the common frog and the house mouse.

rubric.why: Allium cepa is the scientific name of onion.
rubric.description: Gives the scientific name of onion.

rubric.why: Asterias rubens is a scientific name used for the sea star.
rubric.description: Gives the scientific name of sea star.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Asterias rubens; accept Asterias.

items.followUp: Explain how mitosis helps in the repair of damaged tissues.

rubric.why: Mitosis produces additional cells, increasing cell number for growth.
rubric.description: States that mitosis increases the number of cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that mitosis produces new cells or increases cell number.

rubric.why: The new cells support growth and the development of tissues and organs.
rubric.description: Links mitosis-produced cells with growth and development.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting mitosis with growth or development of the organism, tissues, or organs.

modelAnswer: Mitosis produces new cells, increasing the number of cells in an organism.
This increase in cell number brings about growth and helps in the development of tissues and organs.

items.followUp: What happens during the S phase of interphase?

rubric.why: Cell growth is a key event in G1.
rubric.description: States that the cell grows or increases in size during G1.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing cell growth during G1.

rubric.why: The cell carries out normal metabolism and makes proteins and organelles needed for later stages.
rubric.description: Mentions normal metabolic activity or synthesis of proteins and organelles during G1.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that proteins or organelles are made, or that normal cell activities continue.

modelAnswer: During G1, the cell grows and increases in size.
It carries out normal metabolic activities and synthesises proteins and organelles needed for the next stages of the cell cycle.

items.followUp: What is the role of ATP in cellular activities?

rubric.why: Adenine is the nitrogenous base component of ATP.
rubric.description: Names adenine as an ATP component.

rubric.why: ATP also contains ribose sugar and three phosphate groups.
rubric.description: Names ribose and the three phosphate groups as the remaining ATP components.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying ribose and three phosphate groups.

modelAnswer: ATP consists of the nitrogenous base adenine, the sugar ribose, and three phosphate groups.
Its sub-units are adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups.

items.followUp: Name the two photosystems involved in the Z-scheme and state the source of the electrons.

rubric.why: The Z-scheme describes electron flow during non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
rubric.description: Identifies the Z-scheme as the pathway of electron transport in non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing it as an electron-transport pathway or linking it to non-cyclic photophosphorylation.

rubric.why: The energy-level pattern of electron flow resembles the letter Z.
rubric.description: Explains why it is called the Z-scheme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the energy profile or pathway resembles a Z or zigzag.

modelAnswer: The Z-scheme is the pathway of electron transport during non-cyclic photophosphorylation, involving photosystems II and I.
It is called the Z-scheme because the changes in electron energy along the pathway form a pattern resembling the letter Z.

items.followUp: Explain how temperature can affect enzyme activity.

rubric.why: The model depends on a substrate fitting a specifically shaped enzyme active site.
rubric.description: States that the enzyme has an active site with a shape complementary to a specific substrate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the specific fit between substrate and active site.

rubric.why: The substrate binds temporarily, is converted to product, and the enzyme can be reused.
rubric.description: Describes complex formation and product release while the enzyme remains unchanged.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the enzyme-substrate complex forms and products are released without the enzyme being used up.

modelAnswer: In the lock-and-key model, an enzyme's active site has a specific shape that fits its substrate, like a key fitting a lock.
The substrate binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex; the reaction occurs, products are released, and the enzyme remains unchanged.
